questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What makes a pipeline a pipeline
questions.learningObjective: name what a pipeline is that a single script is not
questions.stem: A team replaces a monthly script with four scheduled steps that hand a table to each other and record when each finished. What has the rewrite added that the script did not have?

options.text: Stages that hand work on, so a failure is located in a step rather than inside one long job
Nothing structural, since the same rows are processed either way and the output is identical
options.misconception: assumes identical output means the two arrangements are equivalent

options.text: A guarantee that each step runs exactly once, which a single script cannot promise about itself
options.misconception: believes splitting a job into steps is what makes a job idempotent

options.text: Automatic recovery, since a step that fails can be rerun on its own without any extra work
options.misconception: believes scheduling stages is the same thing as making retries safe

questions.explanation: A pipeline is a sequence of named steps with recorded boundaries between them, and the boundaries are what make it more than a long job: when a figure is wrong, the boundary is where you look, and a step that failed is a step whose output can be inspected rather than a job that died somewhere in the middle. The rewrite buys observability and locality, not correctness, and it does not by itself make anything run once or recover automatically, both of which are properties of how the steps are written rather than of the fact that there are several of them. That distinction is why splitting a job is often the first change worth making and rarely the last one needed.
questions.hint: Ask what you can do with a failure when you know which step it happened in.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Choosing between batch and streaming
questions.learningObjective: say what decides whether a load can be a stream
questions.stem: A team must keep a feature table current within seconds for a live scoring service, and the source only produces a complete file every night. What does that constraint decide?

options.text: Nothing, because a streaming pipeline can be fed from a file as soon as the file lands
options.misconception: believes the choice between the two styles is independent of what the source produces

options.text: That the load must be batch, since no amount of streaming machinery shortens the gap in the source itself
That the load must be streaming, since a nightly file is only a stream that has not been read yet
options.misconception: reduces a nightly file to a stream by relabelling it

options.text: That the freshness target is negotiable, since no architecture can promise better than its source delivers
options.misconception: concludes the requirement is void rather than the design being wrong

questions.explanation: A pipeline can only be as current as the earliest moment its input exists, so a source that publishes once a night sets a floor of roughly a day no matter how the processing is arranged, and choosing a streaming engine for it adds machinery without moving the number anybody cares about. The reverse case is the one that catches people: a source that emits continuously and a table rebuilt nightly is a stream being throttled, and the fix is usually to consume the events rather than to write a faster batch job. The honest way to run this conversation is to state the freshness target, then ask when the data exists, because those two numbers decide the architecture and nothing else does.
questions.hint: Ask when the input first exists, since no processing can precede that.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a late record does to a window
questions.learningObjective: explain why a late record breaks an already-closed window
questions.stem: A pipeline groups events into one-hour windows and closes a window when its clock passes the hour. An event for 14:05 arrives at 14:47, after the 14:00 window was closed. What happens to that event?

options.text: It is added to the 14:00 window, because the window is defined by the event's own timestamp
options.misconception: believes a closed window can be reopened by a late arrival

options.text: It is dropped or routed to a correction path, because the window it belongs to has already been reported
It starts a new 14:00 window containing only itself, so the totals become two partial windows
options.misconception: assumes a late event opens a second window for the same period

options.text: It replaces the 14:00 window entirely, so the published figures are recomputed with the event included
options.misconception: believes closed windows are provisional until the next event arrives

questions.explanation: A window is closed because something downstream has already consumed its total, and putting a late event back into it would mean a figure changed after it was read, which is the failure mode windows exist to prevent. The event therefore goes to a correction path, a late-data side output, or nowhere, and the choice is a business decision about how much a late arrival is worth rather than a technical detail. What makes this uncomfortable in practice is that the late event is not wrong, and a pipeline that discards it is discarding real activity, which is why the correction path and its reconciliation against the raw stream are worth the extra work.
questions.hint: Ask what downstream has already done with the window by the time the late event arrives.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Duplicates and an idempotent write
questions.learningObjective: say what makes a repeated write safe to repeat
questions.stem: A stream redelivers a batch of events after a consumer restart, so the same event ids arrive twice. What makes the second write harmless?

options.text: Writing under the event's own id so that a repeat replaces the row it already wrote
Checking the row count before writing, so a second attempt against a full table is skipped
options.misconception: believes a size check identifies which rows have already been written

options.text: Writing to a new table each time and reading from the newest, so earlier tables are left intact
options.misconception: assumes keeping old versions of the data makes a repeated write harmless

options.text: Writing only the fields that changed, so a repeat sends an empty update and alters nothing
options.misconception: believes a partial write is the same operation as a full one

questions.explanation: Idempotence means the second attempt leaves the same state as the first, and the only way to get that with duplicated deliveries is to give each event a key the sink can recognise, so a repeat overwrites its own row instead of adding another. The other three are versions of hoping rather than deciding: a row count cannot say which rows are new, a new table per attempt trades duplicates for an unbounded number of tables to reconcile, and a partial write leaves the first attempt's values in place only if every field happens to be unchanged, which is exactly the assumption that failed. The event id has to come from the producer for this to work, which is why an identifier in the contract is worth as much as a schema.
questions.hint: Ask what the sink can recognise about a repeat, and whether anything it can see identifies the event.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Out-of-order events and the watermark
questions.learningObjective: say what a watermark decides about an out-of-order event
questions.stem: Events arrive out of order: the 14:07 event is seen before the 14:03 one. A watermark tracks how far behind the latest event time the stream has fallen. What does it tell the pipeline?

options.text: How late an event may still arrive before its window is treated as complete and closed
How many events have arrived out of order, which is the disorder the pipeline must absorb
options.misconception: confuses the bound on lateness with a count of disordered events

options.text: Which events will arrive late, so the ones already seen can be discarded before their window opens
options.misconception: believes the watermark predicts which specific events will be late

options.text: How long the stream has been running, so a long-running stream can use a wider window than a short one
options.misconception: reads a lateness bound as a measure of elapsed time

questions.explanation: A watermark is a promise about the future made by the pipeline's own state: no event older than this point is still expected. That is precisely what a windowing decision needs, because a window can only be closed once it is safe, and safety here means nobody will add to it later. A larger watermark tolerates more disorder and closes windows later, so there is a direct trade between completeness and latency, and choosing it is a business decision about how much lateness the reporting can absorb. What the watermark never does is predict which events will be late or count the ones that already were, so an event beyond the bound is a genuine surprise and needs a correction path rather than an assumption that it cannot happen.
questions.hint: Ask what the watermark asserts about events that have not arrived yet.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A schema change and the consumer it breaks
questions.learningObjective: say why a compatible-looking change still breaks a consumer
questions.stem: A producer renames a column from amount_cents to amount and keeps the values identical. A downstream consumer that reads the old name stops receiving data. Why?

options.text: The consumer's contract named the old column, and a consumer may only read what its contract promised
The values changed type during the rename, so the old column no longer holds anything the consumer can use
options.misconception: assumes a rename necessarily changes the stored type

options.text: The consumer's schedule was disturbed by the change, so it ran before the new table was ready
options.misconception: explains a naming change through an unrelated timing effect

options.text: The producer deleted the old column, so the consumer's query is now invalid against the table
options.misconception: believes a rename is a deletion of the column it replaced

questions.explanation: A consumer that was written against a contract is entitled to assume the names in it, and a rename is a change to that contract whether or not the values are identical, so the consumer's read fails and the break is total rather than gradual. The type of change matters less than its declaration: a renamed column delivered under a version bump is a legitimate new version, and the consumer's obligation is to move to it, which is why a contract that states versions and a deprecation window turns this from an outage into a scheduled piece of work. A change delivered without either is the same event as far as production is concerned, an unannounced break, and no amount of identical values prevents it.
questions.hint: Ask what the consumer was promised, and whether the change was declared against that promise.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a data contract states
questions.learningObjective: name what belongs in a data contract and what does not
questions.stem: A team writes a document promising that a table will keep its columns, types and meanings, that new fields may be added, and that removals will be announced a quarter ahead. What has the team written?

options.text: A data contract, since it states what consumers may rely on and how that reliance will be broken
A schema dump, since a list of columns and types is what the consumers actually read from
options.misconception: reduces a contract to the part that a schema file already records

options.text: An access policy, since what consumers may rely on is decided by who is allowed to read the table
options.misconception: reads a promise about shape as a statement about permissions

options.text: A service level objective, since the notice period is a promise about timing rather than about contents
options.misconception: confuses a deprecation window with an availability target

questions.explanation: A contract is the part of a schema a consumer may build on, plus the rules for taking it away, and those two halves are what make it different from a description. The types and names are the easy half and are often recorded anyway; the deprecation window is the half that changes behaviour, because it converts a breaking change from an event into a scheduled piece of work that a consumer can plan for. What a contract does not do is describe the data's meaning in prose, guarantee that values are correct, or promise anything about volume, and a document that claims those things will be believed and then relied upon in exactly the ways it cannot support.
questions.hint: Ask what the document permits a consumer to assume, and how that assumption may be withdrawn.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a data quality test can express
questions.learningObjective: separate the checks a data test can make from the ones it cannot
questions.stem: A pipeline runs a test before publishing. Which of these can that test actually decide?

options.text: That the key column holds no duplicates, the amounts are all positive, and no value is outside its stated range
That the amounts are correct, since a rule about their range is enough to establish what they should be
options.misconception: believes a range check establishes the correctness of a value

options.text: That the rows describe real events, since a row passing every rule is by definition a true record
options.misconception: assumes a row satisfying declared rules is therefore factually right

options.text: That nothing important is missing, since every rule the team wrote down has now been checked
options.misconception: equates passing the checks that exist with having checked everything

questions.explanation: A data test can only decide questions whose answers are already written down somewhere: a uniqueness rule, a sign rule, an allowed range, a required field, a referential rule. Those are worth having because they catch the failure that actually happens most often, a column that quietly changes shape between runs, and a test that fails is a signal worth waking somebody for. What no test can do is confirm that a value is the right value, because correctness lives in the world the pipeline observes and the test has no access to it, which is why every one of the three wrong options involves a jump from a declared rule to a real-world fact. A test suite nobody trusts is worse than none, so the discipline is to state plainly what each rule proves.
questions.hint: Ask which of these questions has its answer recorded somewhere the test can read.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a freshness check catches
questions.learningObjective: name the failure a freshness check detects
questions.stem: A daily table is checked by comparing the time its last successful load finished against a target of 30 minutes after the schedule. One morning the check finds the last load finished 47 minutes before the schedule. What has it caught?

options.text: The table is older than agreed, whether the cause is a late start, a slow step or a job that never ran
The table is empty, since a load that finished late must have written nothing at all
options.misconception: assumes lateness and emptiness are the same failure

options.text: The load is wrong, since a job that took longer than agreed must have produced incorrect rows
options.misconception: believes a duration overrun implies a data error

options.text: The schedule is wrong, since the agreed time was set before the table's volume was known
options.misconception: treats a missed target as evidence the target was badly chosen

questions.explanation: Freshness measures the age of the data as a reader experiences it, and it is deliberately indifferent to the cause: a job that started late, a step that ran long, and a job that failed outright all show up as the same symptom, a table older than promised. That indifference is the strength, because the check answers the question a consumer actually has, which is whether they can trust what they are reading now, and it does so without needing to understand the pipeline well enough to diagnose it. What freshness cannot tell you is whether the rows are right, so it belongs beside a content check rather than instead of one, and a table can be perfectly fresh and perfectly wrong.
questions.hint: Ask what the age of the table looks like from the outside under each of the possible causes.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a row-count check cannot see
questions.learningObjective: name an anomaly a row-count check passes
questions.stem: A load is checked by comparing the rows written against the rows expected, within a 2 percent tolerance. Today's load wrote 1,018,000 rows against 1,000,000 expected, so the check passes. What could still be wrong?

options.text: The 18,000 surplus rows could be duplicates of rows already written, offset by 18,000 rows that never arrived
Nothing, since a total inside tolerance is a direct measure of how much data arrived
options.misconception: treats a passing count as proof of completeness

options.text: The values in those rows could be wrong, since a count of rows says nothing about what is inside them
options.misconception: misses that a count check and a content check answer different questions

options.text: Only the scheduling could be wrong, since the content is verified by the count matching the expectation
options.misconception: believes a row count verifies contents as well as volume

questions.explanation: A count is one number, and two errors of opposite sign add up to a number that looks fine, so a duplicated day and a missing day can pass a tolerance check while the table is wrong in both directions at once. This is the specific blind spot that makes a count check necessary and not sufficient, and it is why the useful additions are all cheap and specific: a count of distinct keys against a count of rows catches duplication, and a count of the key values present yesterday but absent today catches loss. Both are single numbers, both can be run on every load, and both catch the class of failure the total cannot see.
questions.hint: Ask what two different mistakes could add up to, and whether the check can tell them apart.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a null-rate check detects
questions.learningObjective: say what a null-rate check detects and what it costs
questions.stem: A check records the share of blanks in a key column each day and pages when it moves more than two percentage points from its training value. It fires this week. What has it detected?

options.text: The column's missingness has shifted, which usually means the source changed shape rather than that rows went missing
Rows have been deleted, since a deleted row would leave a blank behind in the key column
options.misconception: believes a deleted row can leave evidence in another column

options.text: The load has failed, since a partial load is the ordinary cause of a rising blank rate
options.misconception: assumes a distribution shift is always a load failure

options.text: The training data was wrong, since a shift in production invalidates everything the model learned
options.misconception: believes a production change implies the historical data was faulty

questions.explanation: A null rate is a description of a column's shape, and a move in it is a signal that something upstream changed: a new source system, a field that began arriving empty for one region, a parser that stopped filling a default. Its real value is as a drift detector rather than as a data-quality rule, because the blanks may be entirely legitimate and the check is still reporting something that matters, namely that the population the model was fitted on no longer describes the population it is serving. The cost of the check is that it says nothing about which rows are affected, so it is a trigger for investigation rather than a diagnosis, and a team that pages on it without a follow-up ends up muting it.
questions.hint: Ask what a change in the share of blanks says about the column, and what it does not identify.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Alerting on a pipeline failure
questions.learningObjective: choose the alert that a failure actually reaches
questions.stem: A nightly load has failed once in the last month and nobody noticed for two days. Which change to the alerting would have caught it?

options.text: Have the job report its own success or failure to the alerting system, and page when it reports neither
Add a row-count check to the load, so a partial write is caught before the next run
options.misconception: assumes a content check on a table that was never written can fire

options.text: Lower the threshold on the existing data quality tests, so marginal rows trip them more often
options.misconception: believes tightening a rule helps when nothing ran at all

options.text: Have the dashboard read from a backup of the previous day's table, so the page never goes empty
options.misconception: treats hiding the symptom as detecting the failure

questions.explanation: A job that never ran leaves no bad rows for any content check to find, because the table still holds yesterday's correct data, and every check that inspects the table therefore passes on the most serious failure there is. The only signal that distinguishes did not run from ran and produced nothing is a report from the job itself, which is why a success or failure signal from the scheduler, and an alert on the absence of that signal, is the check that closes this gap. Adding a third content check to a pipeline that did not execute buys nothing at all, which is a useful reminder that the checks guarding a pipeline are not interchangeable.
questions.hint: Ask what a check inspecting the table can conclude when the table was never written.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a retry risks
questions.learningObjective: say what a retried job must be true of before it is safe
questions.stem: A job that writes 50,000 rows fails after writing 45,000, and the scheduler retries it from the beginning without clearing the table. What is the result?

options.text: 95,000 rows, because the retry adds a second copy of the 45,000 already written
50,000 rows, because the retry overwrites the rows it wrote the first time
options.misconception: assumes a plain write replaces existing rows rather than adding to them

options.text: 45,000 rows, because the job skips the rows it has already written on the retry
options.misconception: believes a job can tell which of its own rows are already present

options.text: 5,000 rows, because only the work after the failure point is repeated by the retry
options.misconception: assumes a restart from the beginning resumes from where it stopped

questions.explanation: A retry that starts from the beginning re-does the work the first attempt had already completed, and a write that appends does not notice, so the 45,000 rows that succeeded are now present twice and the table holds 95,000. The two properties that make a retry safe are both about what happens before it runs: either the step replaces the whole target, or it is written so that repeating it changes nothing, which is the same idempotence that protects a stream from redelivery. Retrying is usually the right response to a transient failure, so the fix is not to stop retrying but to make the destination tolerate being written twice, because the next failure will be retried too.
questions.hint: Ask what a plain append does to rows that are already there.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a backfill needs its own path
questions.learningObjective: say why a backfill cannot be the daily job run differently
questions.stem: A pipeline must rebuild 182 days of history that a broken change left unwritten. Why does this need a path of its own rather than a longer-running daily job?

options.text: It must read a different range of the source and write over existing rows, while the daily job must not touch what is already there
It can reuse the daily job unchanged, since the only difference between the two is how long the range is
options.misconception: believes volume is the only thing that separates a backfill from a normal run

options.text: It must skip its quality checks, because historical data is known to be worse than the current day's
options.misconception: assumes older data should be exempt from the checks that protect current data

options.text: It must run against a copy of the source, since the source can only be read once per day by design
options.misconception: invents a source limitation that the daily job would also be subject to

questions.explanation: A backfill differs from a daily run in the direction of its writes: the daily job appends one new day and must leave the rest alone, while a backfill rewrites days that already hold rows and must produce the same result the daily job would have produced. That is a different contract with the destination table, and the difference shows up as duplicated rows, stale rows left behind a corrected change, and a run that reads far more than a day and therefore needs a different set of timeouts. It also needs its own reconciliation, because the evidence that a backfill worked is a per-day comparison against what the pipeline would have produced, not a single total at the end.
questions.hint: Ask in which direction each run writes, and what that implies about rows that are already there.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: End-to-end time of a staged pipeline
questions.learningObjective: compute the wall-clock duration of a sequential pipeline
questions.stem: A daily pipeline runs four stages in sequence: extract takes 4 minutes, validate 2 minutes, transform 9 minutes and load 6 minutes. Assuming no overlap between stages, how many minutes pass between the first stage starting and the last stage finishing?
questions.explanation: Sequential stages add, so 4 + 2 + 9 + 6 = 21 minutes. The second route groups the stages instead of listing them: extract and validate together are 6 minutes, transform and load together are 15, and 6 + 15 = 21, which agrees. The figure that matters operationally is not this total but the pair that bounds it, since the freshness a consumer sees is set by when the load finishes rather than when the pipeline starts, so a pipeline that begins on the hour and takes 21 minutes delivers its data 21 minutes late no matter how the stages are arranged. That is also the number to compare against a freshness target before deciding whether the target is realistic.
questions.hint: Add the stage durations, then check by pairing the first two and the last two.

questions.topic: How far past target a table is
questions.learningObjective: compute a freshness overrun against an agreed target
questions.stem: A daily table is meant to be no more than 30 minutes old. The last successful load finished 47 minutes before the scheduled time. By how many minutes has the table missed its freshness target?
questions.explanation: The overrun is 47 − 30 = 17 minutes. The second route counts the minutes individually: of the 47 minutes that have passed, the first 30 were within the target and minutes 31 through 47 are the 17 that were not, which agrees. The distinction worth holding on to is between a table that is late and a table that is wrong, because the same 17 minutes could have been spent on a job that ran perfectly or on one that failed silently, and only a report from the job itself distinguishes those two cases. A freshness check therefore says the promise was missed and leaves the reason to be established separately.

questions.topic: Movement in a null rate
questions.learningObjective: compute the change in a null rate between two snapshots
questions.stem: In a training snapshot of 500,000 rows, a key column held 10,000 blanks. In today's extract of 60,000 rows, that column holds 4,500 blanks. By how many percentage points has the blank rate moved?
questions.explanation: The training blank rate is 10,000 out of 500,000, which is 2.0 percent, and today's rate is 4,500 out of 60,000, which is 7.5 percent, so the movement is 7.5 − 2.0 = 5.5 percentage points. The second route computes both rates from their numerators directly, 4,500 as a percentage of 60,000 less 10,000 as a percentage of 500,000, and reaches the same 5.5. The two extract sizes are what make this worth doing carefully, because a team comparing raw blank counts would see 4,500 against 10,000, conclude the column improved, and be wrong by more than a factor of two, since the two numbers were never about the same quantity.

questions.stem: A load is expected to write 1,000,000 rows and its check fails when the count is more than 2 percent away from that. Today it wrote 1,018,000 rows. What percentage deviation does the check measure?

The second route divides first and subtracts one, so 1,018,000 out of 1,000,000 is 1.018 and 1.018 − 1 = 0.018, the same 1.8 percent. At 1.8 percent the check passes its 2 percent tolerance, which is exactly why this figure is interesting: the load wrote more rows than expected, and a check written only to catch dramatic losses will wave through a surplus just as readily as a shortfall, even though a surplus of this shape is often a duplicated day arriving on top of a correct one.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Requests a canary receives
questions.learningObjective: compute the traffic a canary share sends to a new model
questions.stem: A release sends 5 percent of live traffic to a candidate model while the rest stays on the current one. During a window carrying 2,000,000 requests, how many requests reach the candidate?
questions.explanation: One twentieth of 2,000,000 is 100,000, since 5 percent is one part in twenty. The second route divides instead of multiplying, and 2,000,000 divided by 20 is the same 100,000. The number is not only a routing detail, because it sets what the canary can detect: with 100,000 requests, an error rate of 0.62 percent is roughly 620 failures, which is a rate that can be told apart from a 0.5 percent baseline, while the same error rate spread over a thousand requests would be six failures and no conclusion at all. Choosing a share is therefore choosing how much evidence the release gets before it has to decide.
questions.hint: Take one part in twenty of the request count, and confirm by dividing by twenty.

questions.topic: Error rate a canary measures
questions.learningObjective: compute a canary's error rate from its own request and failure counts
questions.stem: A candidate model served 100,000 requests during a canary window and 620 of them failed. The current model over the same window failed 0.5 percent of requests. What is the candidate's error rate, as a percentage?

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: An honest limitation against a hedge
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a stated limitation from a disclaimer that protects nobody
questions.stem: Explain what separates a limitation stated honestly from a hedge that protects the writer instead of the reader, and give the sentence that fails.

answer.exemplar: A limitation names a specific population, condition or use where the model should not be relied on, and a hedge attaches uncertainty to the writer rather than to the model's reach. The honest sentence says the performance figures were measured on accounts opened in the last twelve months and says nothing about older accounts, so a reader knows exactly which rows the evidence covers. The failing sentence says the results may vary and that the model is intended for general use, which commits the team to the widest possible claim while warning about none of it, and whose only function is to be quotable in a later dispute. The difference is not tone but addressability: a limitation can be checked against a population and acted on by deciding not to use the model there, whereas a hedge can be applied to any objection at all and therefore disposes of none. It is worth noting that honest limits are also cheaper for the team, because a limit stated in advance is a boundary somebody agreed to, while a limit discovered after an incident is a failure with a name attached to it.

questions.explanation: The test is whether the sentence can be acted on by somebody who was not in the room when it was written. A limitation that names a population gives a reader a decision to make, and a hedge gives them nothing to do except worry, which is why the hedge is preferred by the writer and useless to everyone else. Both protect against being wrong, but only one of them changes what anybody does, and the difference shows up months later when the question is whether the model was ever supposed to be used on those rows at all.
questions.hint: Ask whether the sentence tells a reader where not to rely on the model, or merely tells the writer they are covered.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why an undefined metric cannot be improved
questions.learningObjective: explain what is missing from a metric that has no written definition
questions.stem: Explain why a dashboard metric that nobody has written a definition for cannot be improved by changing the tool that displays it, and say what the definition must contain.

answer.exemplar: A dashboard renders whatever its query returns, so changing the tool changes the rendering and leaves the quantity exactly as undefined as it was, and a prettier panel around an undefined number makes the number more authoritative rather than better defined. The disagreement between two teams is the evidence, since each computed something real and neither can be shown to have computed the wrong thing. The definition has four parts and no more: the entity the row is about, the event that is counted, the window the count covers, and the filter that decides which rows are in scope. Written once and attached to the dashboard rather than to a document, those four sentences end the argument permanently, and until they exist the honest description of the panel is that it displays two metrics that share a label. The temptation to resolve such a disagreement by declaring one team's version canonical is worth resisting, because the reason the two differ is usually that the label has been doing two jobs for a year, and canonising one of them hides a real ambiguity rather than settling it.

questions.explanation: The reason a display change cannot help is that the ambiguity is upstream of the display, so any improvement to the panel is a change to the presentation of a quantity that has not been agreed. Two teams disagreeing is therefore the most valuable thing on the dashboard, because it is the only evidence that the label has been doing two jobs, and silencing it by declaring one version canonical removes the evidence along with the argument. The four-part definition is short enough to write in a sentence and specific enough that a second team computing the metric from it will get the same number, which is the test a definition has to pass.
questions.hint: Ask what a tool change alters, and which four facts a metric has to name before it names a quantity.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: How a figure misleads without being false
questions.learningObjective: explain how a chart can mislead while every number in it is correct
questions.stem: Explain how a chart can mislead a reader while every number in it is correct, and name two things a reader can check in the picture itself.

answer.exemplar: A chart constrains what the eye compares, so the same correct numbers read differently depending on the window, the scale and the ordering, and the misleading happens in the presentation rather than in the data. A vertical axis beginning just above the final value turns a three-quarter fall in error rate into what looks like a cliff, a window chosen to begin on a good day makes a flat series look like a recovery, and a paired series drawn on two different scales invites a comparison between quantities that were never commensurable. None of these is a lie, which is precisely why they survive review, since a reviewer checking the figures finds them all correct. Two things a reader can check in the picture itself cost nothing: whether the axis begins at zero when the mark is a bar whose length is the value, and whether a truncated axis is labelled with its range so the reader can see the choice. A third habit belongs to the author rather than the reader, which is to state the two endpoints in the caption as well, since a caption saying 4.0 percent to 1.0 percent makes the truncation harmless.

questions.explanation: The deception lives in what the eye is asked to compare rather than in any figure, which is why a review that checks numbers finds nothing to object to. Every one of the three devices, a truncated axis, a chosen window and a mismatched pair of scales, changes the comparison while leaving the data intact, and all three are recoverable by a reader who knows to look. That is the useful conclusion: the defences are small and specific, an axis that starts at zero for bars, a labelled range for truncated lines, and the two endpoints repeated in the caption, and they cost nothing while removing most of the room in which a chart can mislead.
questions.hint: Ask what the chart constrains the eye to compare, and what a reader can verify without seeing the data.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A conclusion the analysis cannot carry
questions.learningObjective: explain what an analysis must have done to support a causal claim
questions.stem: Explain why a comparison between two groups found in the data does not by itself support a causal claim, and say what the analysis would need.

answer.exemplar: A comparison between two groups describes how they differed, and the groups were formed by what people did rather than by what was done to them, so any factor that both raises the likelihood of the behaviour and the likelihood of the outcome will produce the same difference with no causal story at all. In the export-button case a plausible alternative is that the customers who press a button labelled export are, by their job, the ones who were already going to complete, which makes the 11 against 8 a statement about two kinds of customer rather than about a button. A larger sample would not help, because it sharpens the estimate of a difference that was never a controlled comparison, and this is the most persistent confusion in reporting, because precision is mistaken for identification. What the analysis needs is either a mechanism that cannot act any other way, a design that assigned the behaviour, or a comparison that holds the plausible alternative fixed, and where none of those is available the honest wording is that the two groups differed, with the candidate explanations named, and the causal claim left for a test that was actually run.

questions.explanation: The gap is between measuring a difference and identifying its cause, and only the first is achieved by comparing groups that formed themselves. Everything the causal claim needs, a mechanism, an assignment, or a comparison holding the alternative fixed, is absent from an observational contrast, and none of them can be supplied by collecting more rows of the same kind. This is worth separating clearly in a report because the two achievements are often confused in both directions: dismissing the comparison because it is observational throws away a real and useful association, while promoting it to causation puts a claim in a document that no one can later defend.
questions.hint: Ask what else could differ between the two groups besides the thing the claim names.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A reliability claim the history contradicts
questions.learningObjective: explain how an aggregate reliability figure hides the history that matters
questions.stem: Explain why a quarterly success rate of 93.3 percent is a poor basis for a reliability claim, and say what should be reported alongside it.

answer.exemplar: An aggregate over ninety runs is an average of months in which the job never failed and months in which it failed every night, and the average of those two histories is a number that describes neither, so a reader who sees 93.3 percent learns something true and something actionable only by accident. What the average hides is the shape, and the shape is what an on-call rota and a consumer of the data actually experience: the worst streak, the longest recent run of successes, and whether the failures cluster. Those three say whether the pipeline is dependable now, which the quarterly figure cannot, and they are cheap to compute from a log that is already being kept. There is a second reason to distrust the aggregate here, which is that a run that fails without being noticed is not counted as a failure by anything except the job's own report, so an aggregate built from visible errors understates the problem by exactly the number of silent failures, and a team that has never instrumented that distinction is reading a figure about a job rather than about the data.

questions.explanation: An aggregate over a quarter is a summary of ninety runs, and the two histories that produce the same summary, one healthy month beside one broken month, and steady quiet failure, are indistinguishable in it. What a reader needs in order to act is the shape of the distribution rather than its centre, so the worst streak and the recent record belong beside the rate, and both come from a log nobody has to start collecting today. The second problem with the figure is that it may be counting only the failures that announced themselves, which makes it a statistic about the job's logging rather than about the data's availability.
questions.hint: Ask what months the average is averaging, and what a reader would want to know that the average cannot say.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: An environment that drifts from the record
questions.learningObjective: explain how an unpinned environment breaks reproducibility without breaking anything visible
questions.stem: Explain how an environment that resolves versions differently from the committed pin breaks reproducibility while every run still appears to succeed, and say what closes the gap.

answer.exemplar: A pin is a claim about the future that only holds if something checks it, and an environment that resolves its own versions turns that claim into a suggestion, so a run performed today and a run performed next quarter are two different computations that share a name. Nothing about this announces itself: the job exits successfully, the metrics come out in a plausible range, and the report looks the same as last month's, which is why the drift is usually discovered when somebody tries to regenerate an old figure and cannot get the same number. The failure is worst for the results nobody re-ran, since a model that quietly changed behaviour after a dependency moved leaves no trace in its own outputs, and the only evidence is a comparison nobody made at the time. The gap closes by recording the resolved versions beside the outputs rather than merely pinning them in a file, because a pin describes an intention while a resolved list describes the environment that actually ran, and a container image or a fully pinned environment closes it more durably by making the two impossible to differ.

questions.explanation: The environment is the one link in the chain from code to result that nothing about the result reveals, because a run under different versions produces output of the same shape and a plausible size, and there is no marker in the numbers saying the ground moved. That is why a pin in a repository is not sufficient on its own: it describes an intention that only a check or a fully pinned image can enforce, and the artefact that actually documents a run is the list of versions that were resolved when it happened. Recording that list beside the outputs is cheap, and it is the difference between a result that can be explained when it surprises somebody and one that has to be regenerated and hoped for.
questions.hint: Ask what a pin promises, and what evidence would show whether the promise was kept.
